title: Vitamin B12 and Alcohol: Depletion, Hangovers, and B12 Shots
excerpt: Does alcohol deplete vitamin B12? How heavy drinking affects B12 absorption and storage, signs of deficiency, and whether B12 pills or shots help a hangover.
metaDescription: Does alcohol deplete B12? How drinking affects absorption, signs of low B12, whether B12 pills or shots help a hangover, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** alcohol and vitamin B12 are safe to take together, and there's no dangerous interaction between them. The real relationship runs the other way: heavy, regular drinking can slowly wear down your body's ability to absorb and store B12, and it can make a B12 blood test harder to read. For an occasional social drinker, B12 status usually isn't affected in any meaningful way. And despite how often it's sold as a hangover fix, there is no good evidence that a B12 pill, shot, or IV drip relieves a hangover in someone who isn't deficient.

**The quick rules:** If you drink moderately and eat a normal diet that includes animal foods or fortified foods, you probably don't need extra B12 because of alcohol. If you drink heavily on a regular basis, eat a vegan diet, are over 50, take metformin or a daily acid reducer, or have had stomach surgery, it's worth asking your doctor about a B12 check. If you want to try B12 for a hangover, it's very unlikely to hurt you, but don't expect it to do the work of water, food, sleep, and drinking less.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and official nutrition guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before taking high-dose B12 if** you have kidney disease, take prescription medication, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have been diagnosed with a blood disorder. **See a doctor soon if** you have ongoing numbness or tingling in your hands or feet, trouble with balance, unusual tiredness and shortness of breath, a sore red tongue, or new problems with memory or mood. **Get emergency care right away (call 911 in the US) if** someone who drinks heavily becomes confused, very unsteady on their feet, or develops strange eye movements or double vision. Those can be signs of a different and urgent vitamin problem, explained below.

## How Alcohol Affects Vitamin B12: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Vitamin B12, also called cobalamin, is a nutrient your body needs to make healthy red blood cells, keep nerves working, and copy DNA. You can't make it yourself. You get it from animal foods such as meat, fish, eggs, and dairy, or from fortified foods and supplements.

Getting B12 from food into your bloodstream is one of the more complicated trips any nutrient takes. It goes roughly like this:

1. **Stomach acid frees it from food.** B12 in food is bound to proteins. Acid and digestive enzymes in the stomach release it.
2. **A carrier protein picks it up.** Cells in the stomach lining produce a protein called intrinsic factor. B12 has to bind to it to be absorbed properly.
3. **The end of the small intestine absorbs it.** The B12 and intrinsic factor pair is absorbed in the last section of the small intestine.
4. **The liver stores it.** Your liver holds the body's main B12 reserve, and that reserve is large. In most people it can last for years, which is why B12 deficiency develops slowly.

Heavy, long-term drinking can interfere at several points along that path:

- **It irritates the stomach lining.** Regular heavy drinking is a common cause of gastritis, which is inflammation of the stomach lining. An inflamed stomach can produce less acid and less intrinsic factor, so less B12 gets released and picked up.
- **It can affect the gut.** Alcohol can damage the lining of the small intestine and change the balance of gut bacteria, which may reduce how well nutrients are absorbed.
- **It can damage the liver, where B12 is stored.** In alcohol-related liver disease, the liver may not hold onto its B12 reserve the way a healthy liver does.
- **It often comes with a poorer diet.** People who drink heavily tend to get more of their calories from alcohol and fewer from nutrient-rich food. That's often the biggest factor of all.

The key word in every point is *heavy* and *long-term*. A few drinks on a Saturday night won't drain a reserve that's measured in years. This is a slow problem tied to drinking patterns, not to any single night out.

## Does Alcohol Actually Cause B12 Deficiency?

It can contribute to it, but B12 is not the vitamin alcohol hits hardest, and the picture is more mixed than many supplement websites suggest.

Research on people who drink heavily has found a range of B12 results. Some studies find lower B12 status, while others find normal or even **higher than normal** B12 levels in the blood. That second finding surprises people, and it matters.

### Why your B12 blood test might look fine when it isn't

When liver cells are damaged, they can release some of their stored B12 into the bloodstream. That pushes the blood level up even though the body's reserve may be shrinking and the B12 may not be reaching tissues well. Doctors have noted for a long time that unusually high blood B12 can show up alongside liver disease, which is one reason a high B12 result is sometimes treated as a reason to look at the liver rather than as good news.

The practical upshot: a standard serum B12 test can be misleading in someone who drinks heavily. If a doctor suspects a problem, they may order additional tests, such as **methylmalonic acid (MMA)** and **homocysteine**, which tend to rise when your cells aren't getting enough B12. These give a better picture of whether B12 is actually doing its job.

### The other "big red cells" story

Heavy drinking commonly causes red blood cells to become larger than normal, which shows up on a routine blood count as a high MCV (mean corpuscular volume). B12 and folate deficiency can cause the same thing. So a high MCV in someone who drinks a lot could come from alcohol itself, from low folate, from low B12, or from a mix. Only testing can tell them apart, which is another reason not to self-diagnose.

### The vitamins alcohol depletes more often

If you're worried about alcohol and vitamins, B12 is not usually the first one doctors think about. Two others are more commonly affected:

- **Folate (vitamin B9).** Alcohol interferes with how folate is absorbed, used, and stored, and folate stores are much smaller than B12 stores, so they run out faster. Low folate is common in people who drink heavily.
- **Thiamine (vitamin B1).** This is the most serious one. Alcohol reduces thiamine absorption, and the body stores very little. Severe thiamine deficiency can cause Wernicke's encephalopathy, a medical emergency that affects the brain. Its classic signs are confusion, unsteady walking, and abnormal eye movements. It needs urgent hospital treatment with thiamine, not a supplement at home.

So if you drink heavily on a regular basis, a doctor will usually look at the whole B-vitamin picture, not just B12. Our guide to [vitamins for hangovers](/never-hungover/vitamins-for-hangover) covers how the other vitamins fit into the alcohol story.

## Signs of Low B12 to Watch For

B12 deficiency comes on slowly, sometimes over years, and the early signs are easy to blame on stress, sleep, or a busy week. Common signs include:

- **Tiredness and weakness** that doesn't improve with rest
- **Pale or slightly yellow skin**
- **Shortness of breath or a racing heart** with light activity, from anemia
- **Pins and needles, numbness, or tingling** in the hands and feet
- **Problems with balance or coordination**
- **A sore, smooth, red tongue** or mouth ulcers
- **Memory problems, trouble concentrating, low mood, or irritability**

The nerve symptoms deserve special attention. Tingling or numbness that lasts, or balance that's getting worse, should be checked by a doctor rather than treated on your own. Nerve damage from B12 deficiency can become permanent if it goes on long enough, and catching it early matters.

There's also an overlap problem for drinkers. Heavy alcohol use can cause nerve damage on its own, called alcoholic neuropathy, which also shows up as tingling, burning, or numbness in the feet and hands. B12 deficiency, thiamine deficiency, and alcohol itself can all play a part, and often more than one is involved. That's a job for a doctor and some blood tests, not guesswork.

### Who is most at risk of low B12

Alcohol is only one of many reasons people run low. You're more likely to need a B12 check if you:

- **Drink heavily on a regular basis**
- **Eat a vegan or mostly plant-based diet** without fortified foods or a supplement
- **Are over 50.** Many older adults make less stomach acid, which makes it harder to free B12 from food.
- **Take metformin** for diabetes. Long-term use is linked with lower B12 levels.
- **Take acid reducers every day**, such as proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole, esomeprazole) or H2 blockers (famotidine), for long periods
- **Have had weight-loss surgery** or surgery on the stomach or small intestine
- **Have a gut condition** such as Crohn's disease or celiac disease
- **Have pernicious anemia**, an autoimmune condition in which the body stops making enough intrinsic factor

If you tick a couple of these boxes and you also drink most days, the combination is worth mentioning to your doctor.

## B12 for a Hangover: Does It Work?

This is the question most people actually search for, so here's a direct answer: **there is no good evidence that B12 relieves or prevents hangovers in people who aren't deficient.**

B12 shows up in a lot of hangover products, energy drinks, and "recovery" formulas, and the reasoning sounds plausible. B12 is involved in energy metabolism, alcohol can affect B vitamins, and a hangover leaves you exhausted, so topping up B12 should help. The trouble is that each link in that chain is weak:

- **A single night of drinking doesn't drain your B12.** Your liver's reserve is large enough to cover years of normal needs. One evening won't make a dent you'd notice the next morning.
- **B12 doesn't give energy to people who already have enough.** It helps your body *use* energy from food. If your levels are normal, adding more doesn't create extra energy. The "B12 energy boost" is mostly a real effect only in people who were deficient to begin with.
- **The main causes of a hangover are elsewhere.** Hangovers are driven by things like poor sleep, inflammation, dehydration, the toxic alcohol by-product acetaldehyde, and irritation of the stomach. B12 doesn't target any of those directly.

What does the research on hangover remedies say overall? A systematic review published in the *BMJ* in 2005 looked at randomized trials of hangover treatments and found no compelling evidence that any of them worked. More recent reviews have reached similar conclusions: a few remedies have small, low-quality studies behind them, but none has strong proof. B12 specifically has not been shown to help in a controlled trial that we know of.

Some dietary research has looked at whether people who eat more of certain nutrients report milder hangovers. A 2019 study from researchers in the Netherlands, published in the *Journal of Clinical Medicine*, linked higher dietary intake of zinc and niacin (vitamin B3) with less severe hangovers. That's an interesting observation, but it was about everyday diet, not a hangover-morning dose, and B12 wasn't one of the nutrients that stood out.

### Why people swear by it anyway

If B12 doesn't do much for a hangover, why do so many people say it helps? A few reasons:

- **It usually comes with other things.** A "B12 hangover drink" often includes water, sugar, electrolytes, or caffeine. Those can make you feel better, and B12 gets the credit.
- **Hangovers get better on their own.** Whatever you take in the morning, you'll usually feel better by the afternoon.
- **Expectation matters.** If you believe something will help, you're more likely to notice improvement. That's a real effect, but it isn't the vitamin.
- **Some people are low without knowing it.** If you're one of them, B12 may genuinely help your energy over days and weeks, though not your hangover that morning.

None of this means B12 is harmful. If you take a B-complex or a B12 tablet and like your routine, it's very unlikely to hurt you. Just don't count on it to undo a heavy night.

## B12 Shots for a Hangover

B12 injections are a real medical treatment. Doctors use them for people with confirmed deficiency, especially when the gut can't absorb B12 well, such as in pernicious anemia or after some kinds of stomach surgery. In those patients, injections work very well.

The "B12 shot for your hangover" offered by some wellness clinics and IV lounges is a different thing. Here's what it does and doesn't do:

- **If you're not deficient, most of it leaves in your urine.** B12 is water-soluble. When your stores are already full, your body holds onto only a small part of a large dose and the kidneys clear much of the rest. Some forms can even tint your urine pink or red for a day or two.
- **It won't speed up alcohol clearance.** Nothing in a B12 shot changes how fast your liver breaks down alcohol or its by-products.
- **The feeling of relief often comes from the fluids.** Many "hangover IV" packages include a bag of saline, sometimes with anti-nausea or pain medication. Fluids can genuinely help a dehydrated person feel better. The B12 is along for the ride.
- **It costs real money.** A single shot or drip session often runs from tens of dollars into the low hundreds, for a benefit you could mostly get from water, an electrolyte drink, food, and sleep.

B12 injections are generally considered safe, but any injection carries small risks such as pain, bruising, or, rarely, an allergic reaction. If a clinic is giving IV fluids, make sure qualified medical staff are involved and that they ask about your health history and medications.

### Shots versus pills for actual deficiency

If you do turn out to be low in B12, you may not need injections at all. For many people, high-dose oral B12 works well. Even without intrinsic factor, a small fraction of a large oral dose gets absorbed passively through the gut wall, and at high doses that small fraction adds up to enough. Your doctor will choose between shots and tablets based on why you're low and how severe it is. That's a decision to make with them, not at a drip bar.

## Is It Safe to Take B12 Supplements While Drinking?

Yes, for nearly everyone. There's no known harmful interaction between a standard B12 supplement and alcohol. A few practical notes:

- **You can take it the same day you drink.** There's no need to space them apart. If you take B12 for a diagnosed deficiency, keep taking it as directed.
- **Absorption may be a bit worse in heavy drinkers.** That's one reason doctors sometimes use injections or higher oral doses for people with alcohol-related gut or liver problems.
- **More isn't better.** The recommended daily amount for most adults is 2.4 micrograms, according to the US National Institutes of Health. Supplements often contain hundreds or thousands of micrograms. No official upper limit has been set because B12 has low toxicity, but that doesn't make megadoses useful if you're not deficient.
- **Check with your doctor if you have kidney disease.** People with kidney problems should get advice before taking high-dose B vitamins, including the cyanocobalamin form found in many supplements.
- **Watch the rest of the label.** Some "hangover" B12 products also contain caffeine, large doses of niacin, or other ingredients. High-dose niacin can cause flushing and, in large amounts over time, strain the liver, which is not what you want on top of alcohol.

### Which form of B12 is best?

You'll see several forms on supplement labels:

- **Cyanocobalamin:** the most common and most studied form in supplements and fortified foods. It's stable and inexpensive.
- **Methylcobalamin:** a form your body uses directly. It's often marketed as "more natural" or "better absorbed."
- **Hydroxocobalamin:** commonly used in injections, especially outside the US.
- **Adenosylcobalamin:** another active form, often paired with methylcobalamin.

For a healthy person, there's no strong evidence that one form is clearly better than another for keeping B12 levels normal. The body converts each of them into the active forms it needs. Pick a reputable brand with third-party testing and don't pay a big premium for the label claim.

## A Word on Nitrous Oxide

This one is relevant to party settings, so it's worth saying plainly. Recreational nitrous oxide, often sold as "whippets," "nangs," or in balloons, inactivates vitamin B12 in the body. Repeated or heavy use has been linked to serious nerve and spinal cord damage from functional B12 deficiency, even in young people with normal diets. Combining it with alcohol also raises the risk of falls, fainting, and accidents.

If you've used nitrous oxide regularly and notice tingling, numbness, weakness in your legs, or trouble walking, see a doctor promptly and tell them about the nitrous use. Early treatment matters, and taking a B12 supplement at home is not a substitute for proper care.

## How to Keep Your B12 Healthy If You Drink

For most people who drink socially, keeping B12 in a good range comes down to ordinary habits:

1. **Eat B12-rich foods regularly.** The best sources include clams, beef liver, fish such as salmon, trout, and tuna, beef, eggs, milk, yogurt, and cheese. If you eat little or no animal food, look for fortified breakfast cereals, fortified plant milks, or fortified nutritional yeast, or take a supplement.
2. **Keep drinking moderate.** Most of the absorption and storage problems described above come from heavy, long-term drinking. Staying within moderate limits protects your stomach, gut, and liver, and with them your B12.
3. **Don't drink on an empty stomach.** Eating before and while you drink is easier on your stomach lining and helps with almost every part of the next morning. Something like [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) also happens to be a decent B12 source.
4. **Ask about testing if you're in a risk group.** If you drink most days and also take metformin or a daily acid reducer, are over 50, or eat a vegan diet, ask your doctor whether a B12 check makes sense. Mention your drinking honestly so they know which tests to order and how to read them.
5. **Think about the other nutrients too.** Magnesium, folate, and thiamine are more often affected by alcohol than B12. Our guide on [magnesium and alcohol](/never-hungover/magnesium-and-alcohol) covers one of the most common gaps.

## When to See a Doctor

> **For social drinkers, most B12 questions can wait for a routine appointment. Some can't.**
>
> **Book an appointment soon if:** you have tingling, numbness, or burning in your hands or feet that lasts more than a few days; your balance is getting worse; you feel unusually tired and short of breath for weeks; you have a sore, smooth, red tongue; or you notice new problems with memory, focus, or mood.
>
> **Get emergency care right away (call 911 in the US) if:** someone who drinks heavily becomes confused, very unsteady, or develops abnormal eye movements or double vision (possible Wernicke's encephalopathy, which needs urgent thiamine treatment in hospital); or someone has shaking, sweating, seeing or hearing things that aren't there, or a seizure after cutting back on heavy daily drinking, since alcohol withdrawal can be dangerous and needs medical care.
>
> A doctor can run the right tests, sort out whether alcohol, a vitamin, or something else is behind your symptoms, and treat the cause.

## A Better Plan for the Morning After

If you're searching for B12 because you keep waking up tired and foggy after drinking, the vitamin probably isn't the missing piece. The things with the best support are simple: pace yourself, alternate alcoholic drinks with water, eat a real meal, and protect your sleep. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through each one, and if you wake up trembling, our piece on [hangover shakes](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes) explains what's going on.

Some people also add **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, and the human evidence is still limited, so think of it as promising rather than proven. It isn't a substitute for drinking less, and there's no good evidence that it prevents B12 or other vitamin depletion. If you want to try it, [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) combines DHM with a B-complex and other ingredients, while [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a simpler, budget-friendly option that's mostly just DHM. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands side by side.

## The Bottom Line

- B12 and alcohol are safe to take together. There's no harmful interaction.
- Heavy, long-term drinking can reduce how well you absorb and store B12, mainly through stomach, gut, and liver damage and a poorer diet. Occasional social drinking usually doesn't.
- B12 blood tests can look normal or even high in people with alcohol-related liver damage, so doctors may use extra tests such as MMA and homocysteine.
- Folate and thiamine are more often depleted by alcohol than B12, and severe thiamine deficiency is a medical emergency.
- There is no good evidence that B12 pills, shots, or IV drips relieve hangovers in people who aren't deficient.
- If you have lasting tingling, numbness, balance problems, or unusual fatigue, see a doctor rather than self-treating.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you take vitamin B12 and drink alcohol?**

Yes. There's no known harmful interaction between a standard B12 supplement and alcohol, and you don't need to space them apart. If you take B12 for a diagnosed deficiency, keep taking it as your doctor directed. People with kidney disease should ask their doctor before taking high-dose B vitamins.

**Does alcohol deplete vitamin B12?**

Heavy, long-term drinking can lower B12 by irritating the stomach lining (which reduces the acid and carrier protein needed for absorption), damaging the gut and liver, and crowding out nutritious food. Occasional or moderate drinking usually doesn't make a meaningful difference, because the liver stores enough B12 to last a long time. Alcohol tends to affect folate and thiamine more than B12.

**Does B12 help with a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that B12 relieves or prevents hangovers in people who aren't deficient. A single night of drinking doesn't drain your B12 stores, and extra B12 doesn't add energy if your levels are already normal. Products that seem to help often also contain water, electrolytes, sugar, or caffeine, which are more likely to explain the effect.

**Do B12 shots work for hangovers?**

B12 shots are an effective treatment for confirmed deficiency, but there's no good evidence they help a hangover in someone with normal levels. If your stores are full, much of the dose is cleared in your urine. When a hangover IV makes people feel better, the fluids, and sometimes added anti-nausea or pain medicine, are the more likely reason.

**Why is my B12 high if I drink a lot?**

When liver cells are damaged, they can release stored B12 into the blood, which can push the blood level up even if the body's reserve is shrinking. Unusually high B12 is sometimes a reason for a doctor to check the liver. If you drink heavily and your B12 comes back high, talk to your doctor about what it means rather than assuming it's good news.

**What are the signs of B12 deficiency in drinkers?**

The signs are the same as in anyone: lasting tiredness, pale skin, shortness of breath, tingling or numbness in the hands and feet, balance problems, a sore red tongue, and changes in memory or mood. In people who drink heavily, alcohol itself and low thiamine can cause similar nerve symptoms, so a doctor and blood tests are needed to find the cause.

**How much B12 should I take if I drink?**

Most adults need 2.4 micrograms a day, which a normal diet with animal or fortified foods usually provides. There's no special dose for drinkers. If you're in a higher-risk group, such as regular heavy drinking, a vegan diet, age over 50, or long-term metformin or acid reducer use, ask your doctor about testing before choosing a dose, since treating a true deficiency often needs much more than the daily amount.
